payload.body: The submediant is scale degree 6 of a key: the pitch a major sixth above the tonic in a major key and a minor sixth above the tonic in a natural minor key, bearing the submediant function as the subordinate degree of the scale's upper region. In C major the submediant is A (the root of the iv chord, an A-minor triad), and in A natural minor it is F (the root of the VI chord, an F-major triad). (2) functional role — it is the degree that commonly moves to the dominant as a pre-dominant or colour degree (submediant–dominant motion, iv–V or VI–V), and it names the key a third from the tonic (the vi / VI key, one of the keys in mediant relation to the tonic). (3) relational definition — the submediant is defined relative to the tonic (the submediant of C major is A; of A minor is F) and is the sixth ordinal of the key's scale. payload.body: The supertonic is scale degree 2 of a key: the pitch a major second above the tonic (in a major key) or a minor second above the tonic (in a natural minor key), and the bearer of the supertonic function — the degree that moves from the tonic outward toward the pre-dominant region. In C major the supertonic is D (the root of the ii chord, a minor triad), and in A natural minor it is B (the root of the ii° chord, a diminished triad). PARAMETERS: (1) intervallic status — the supertonic sits a major second above the tonic in major keys and a minor second above the tonic in natural minor keys; it is a whole step below the mediant and a whole step above the tonic; (2) functional role — it commonly moves from the tonic to the pre-dominant region (tonic → supertonic → dominant motion, I–ii–V or I–vi–V), and in minor keys the supertonic triad is diminished (ii°) which gives it a leading quality of its own; (3) relational definition — the supertonic is defined relative to the tonic (the supertonic of C major is D; of A minor is B) and is the second ordinal of the key's scale. PERSISTENCE: codified in Western tonal and harmonic theory, taught in music-theory and harmony curricula (scale-degree numbering; Roman-numeral analysis naming ii in major and ii° in minor), reproduced in composition and analysis practice (identifying the supertonic's role in tonic-pre-dominant motion and in deceptive cadences where V resolves to vi — the supertonic's relative key), and maintained through the conventions of tonal notation. Distinctions: from the mediant (scale degree 3 — a third above the tonic, the degree between the tonic and the subdominant; the supertonic occupies the second, not the third, ordinal slot); from the tonic (scale degree 1 — the point of rest that the supertonic leaves; the supertonic is the first step of departure); from a bare pitch (any point on the pitch axis; the supertonic is a pitch bearing the specific second-degree status and the outward function); from the ii chord (the triad built on the second degree — a chord built ON the supertonic, not the degree and function itself). payload.body: The mediant is scale degree 3 of a key: the pitch a major third above the tonic (in a major key) or a minor third above the tonic (in a minor key), and the bearer of the mediant function — the degree that occupies the middle position of the diatonic scale and serves as the shared tone between the tonic and dominant functions. In C major the mediant is E (the root of the iii chord, a minor triad), and in A minor the mediant is C (the root of the I chord, a major triad). PARAMETERS: (1) intervallic status — the mediant sits a major third above the tonic in major keys and a minor third above the tonic in minor keys; it divides the perfect fifth (tonic to dominant) into two thirds, making it the harmonic midpoint of the diatonic fifth; (2) functional role — it is the degree that commonly functions as a weak pre-dominant (moving to the dominant as iii–V or to the tonic as iii–I), and it serves as the shared tone between the tonic triad (I) and the dominant triad (V): in C major, the mediant E is the third of the I chord and the seventh of the V chord, linking them; (3) relational definition — the mediant is defined relative to the tonic (the mediant of C major is E; of A minor is C) and is the third ordinal of the key's scale. payload.body: The mediant is scale degree 3 of a key: the pitch a major third above the tonic (in a major key) or a minor third above the tonic (in a minor key), and the bearer of the mediant function — the degree that occupies the middle position of the diatonic scale and divides the perfect fifth. In C major the mediant is E (the root of the iii chord, a minor triad), and in A minor the mediant is C (the root of the III chord, a major triad). PARAMETERS: (1) intervallic status — the mediant sits a major third above the tonic in major keys and a minor third above the tonic in minor keys; it divides the perfect fifth (tonic to dominant) into two thirds, making it the harmonic midpoint of the diatonic fifth; (2) functional role — it is the degree that commonly functions as a weak pre-dominant (moving to the dominant as iii–V or to the tonic as iii–I); the mediant triad (iii) is a standard pivot chord, sharing two tones with both the tonic triad and the dominant triad (in C major: I = C-E-G and iii = E-G-B share E and G; iii = E-G-B and V = G-B-D share G and B) — it is the chord, not the pitch, that links I and V, and the shared tone of the I and V triads themselves is G, the fifth degree, not the mediant; (3) relational definition — the mediant is defined relative to the tonic (the mediant of C major is E; of A minor is C) and is the third ordinal of the key's scale. PERSISTENCE: codified in Western tonal and harmonic theory, taught in music-theory and harmony curricula (scale-degree numbering; Roman-numeral analysis naming iii in major and III in minor), reproduced in composition and analysis practice (identifying the mediant's pre-dominant and pivot roles in voice-leading and modulation), and maintained through the conventions of tonal notation. Distinctions: from the supertonic (scale degree 2 — a second above the tonic, the first degree of departure; the mediant occupies the third ordinal slot); from the subdominant (scale degree 4 — a fourth above the tonic, the degree of departure; the mediant is below the subdominant); from the dominant (scale degree 5 — the point of tension; the mediant sits a third below it and carries a subordinate role); from a bare pitch (any point on the pitch axis; the mediant is a pitch bearing the specific third-degree status and the middle-function); from the iii chord (the triad built on the third degree — a chord built ON the mediant, not the degree and function itself). payload.body: Infixation is a morphological process in which a language inserts a bound morpheme — an infix — into the interior of a word stem, splitting the stem into two parts that bracket the inserted element. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) the inserted material is a bound morpheme, not an independent word — this is what separates infixation from tmesis, which inserts a grammatically independent word into the same interior position; (2) the insertion occurs at a fixed morphophonological position within the stem (a specific boundary or segment), so the process is a rule of the grammar rather than a free choice of the speaker; (3) the host stem retains its lexical identity, and the infixed form remains analyzable as a variant of that stem. Paradigmatic cases: Tagalog actor-focus infix -um- (kain 'to eat' → k-um-in 'to eat'), and the frequently cited but disputed English -ab- (ab-sent, ab-sole). Infixation persists two ways: as a productive rule — speakers of a language coin new infixed forms on the fly, and the rule survives as long as it is applied — and as a stable category of description — grammars, morphology textbooks, and formal rule specifications continue to state where the infix attaches and what it marks. payload.body: Trousers are a human-made lower-body garment consisting of a waist section and two separate leg sections that descend from the waist, worn as a single unit covering both legs. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) bifurcated construction — two leg sections split at the crotch, in contrast to the single tube of a skirt; (2) leg coverage from the waist downward — full-length trousers carry each leg section to at least the ankle, and variants truncating the legs at the thigh are classified as shorts, an instance of this kind rather than a separate kind; (3) waist fastening — a waistband, drawstring, or closure, with a front fly or other closure. Trousers persist through garment manufacture: the two-legged cut, its tailoring and assembly conventions, and its standard position in dress codes and retail classification are reproduced by tailors and manufacturers and taught as a basic category of dress. payload.body: Tmesis is a morphological operation in which a grammatically independent word or phrase — not a bound morpheme — is inserted into the interior of a single lexical word, splitting it into two parts that bracket the inserted element. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) the inserted material is a free morpheme with its own syntactic independence, distinguishing tmesis from infixation where the inserted material is a bound morpheme; (2) the host word retains its lexical identity and can be recovered by removing the inserted element, making the construction analyzable as a split original; (3) the insertion occurs at a conventionalized position within the host word's internal structure, typically between the first and second syllable or after a specific phoneme, rather than being freely insertable at any point. Paradigmatic cases: the English exclamatory tmesis "fan-frickin'-tastic" (fan + frickin' + tastic), the Greek tmesis in Homer ("κατὰ μοῦνον" split from a compound), and various Oceanic languages where interrogative particles are inserted into verbs. Tmesis persists through discourse convention: the split form becomes recognizable as a unit through repeated usage in expressive or emphatic contexts, and the phenomenon is catalogued in grammars of the languages that exhibit it. [formal: transfixio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: A suffix is a bound morpheme that attaches to the end of a word stem (or base), modifying its meaning, grammatical category, or both. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) position — the morpheme occurs after the stem, in contrast to prefixes (before the stem) and infixes (within the stem); (2) boundness — the suffix cannot occur as an independent word; it requires a host stem to be realized, making it grammatically dependent; (3) function — the suffix either derives a new lexical item (derivational suffix: noun-making -ness, adjective-making -ful) or marks a grammatical feature without changing category (inflectional suffix: plural -s, past tense -ed, comparative -er). Paradigmatic cases: English derivational suffix -ity (active → activity) and inflectional suffix -s (cat → cats); Latin -āre (infinitive marker); Turkish -lar (plural, agglutinative). Suffixes persist through morphological productivity — speakers apply suffix rules to new stems, and the inventory of suffixes is maintained in the grammatical descriptions and lexical entries of each language. [formal: suffixus | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

payload.body: A morpheme is the smallest unit of language that carries meaning or a grammatical function, and cannot be decomposed into smaller meaningful units. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) minimality - a morpheme is the shortest stretch of language that carries meaning or grammatical function on its own; the English word cats decomposes into the two morphemes cat and -s, and no smaller meaningful unit exists below that level; (2) the type-token distinction - a morpheme type is a repeatable unit that recurs across many tokens, and the inventory of types is finite in any given language; (3) the free-bound distinction - a morpheme is either free (it can stand as an independent word: house) or bound (it occurs only within a word: un-, -ness), and every word is composed of one or more morphemes. Paradigmatic cases: the English three-morpheme word unhappiness (un- + happy + -ness), the single-morpheme water, and the agglutinative Turkish evde (ev + de, in the house), where morpheme boundaries are maximally visible. The morpheme persists as a stable category of description: it is the basic unit of morphological analysis, stated in the grammars, textbooks and dictionaries of every language, and reproduced whenever a new word is analyzed. [formal: morphema | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An affix is a bound morpheme that attaches to a host word stem (or base), modifying its meaning or grammatical function. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) boundness - an affix cannot occur as an independent word and is realized only inside a host word, which distinguishes affixes from free morphemes; (2) position - an affix is a prefix (before the stem, as in English un-), a suffix (after the stem, as in English -ness), or an infix (within the stem, as in Tagalog -um-), and the position is a fixed property of the affix in a given language; (3) function - an affix is either derivational (it produces a new lexical item, often of a different category: happy + -ness to happiness) or inflectional (it marks a grammatical feature within a paradigm: plural -s, past -ed). Paradigmatic cases: English -ness (adjective to noun), Latin -are (infinitive marker), Tagalog -um- (actor focus: kain to k-um-in). Affixes persist through morphological productivity - speakers apply affixation rules to new stems, and the inventory of affixes is maintained in the grammatical descriptions and lexical entries of each language. [formal: affixus | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Compounding is a word-formation process that combines two or more independent lexical items (free morphemes) into a single word. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) the components are free - each component is a word that can stand on its own, which distinguishes compounding from affixation (where the attached element is a bound morpheme) and from tmesis (where one independent element is inserted into the interior of a single host word); (2) the result is a single word - the components are juxtaposed and fused into one orthographic and prosodic unit; (3) compositionality - the meaning of a compound ranges from transparent (black + board, blackboard) to idiomatic (many + fold, manifold), and the degree of transparency is a parameter of each particular compound rather than of the process as a whole. Paradigmatic cases: English blackboard and skyscraper; German Haustuer (house + door); Japanese yamane (mountain + ape, monkey). Compounding persists as a productive rule of the grammar - speakers coin new compounds on the fly, and the inventory of compounds is maintained in dictionaries and lexical entries. payload.body: Word formation is the made category comprising the processes by which a language's speakers produce new words from existing lexical material. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) the input is existing lexical material of the language — stems, morphemes, or whole words — which separates word formation from borrowing (which introduces material from another language) and from one-off coinage by a single act of naming; (2) the output is a new word — a new lexical item entering the language's inventory, not a new phrase, sentence, or mere variant of an existing word; (3) the operations are rule-governed in a given language: each language has its own available operations and their combinations, so which formations are possible is a parameter of the grammar, not free invention. Its members include compounding (juxtaposing free morphemes into a single word), affixation (attaching bound morphemes to a stem), infixation (inserting a bound morpheme into a stem's interior), and tmesis (inserting a grammatically independent element into a word's interior); the board's entries for those operations are instances of this genus. Paradigmatic cases: English blackboard (compounding), English -ness (suffixation), Tagalog -um- (infixation: kain 'eat' to k-um-in), fan-frickin'-tastic (tmesis). Word formation persists as a category of grammatical description: its operations are catalogued in the grammars and dictionaries of each language, taught as a stable classification in linguistics, and applied productively by speakers who coin new words.
